turns.t: G'day. I've got dry eyes and a dry mouth, and it's driving me spare.
Right. How long's that been going on?
Three months, about.
Constant, or worse at certain times?
Worse overnight. I wake up with my tongue stuck to the roof of my mouth.
And the eyes. What do they feel like?
Gritty. Like there's sand in them, mostly by the afternoon.
Do you wear contact lenses?
Nah, just glasses for reading and driving.
Fine. What do you do for work?
Call centre. I'm on the phone eight hours a day, talking non-stop.
That'd dry anyone's mouth out, but not usually to this degree. Any history of health problems?
Underactive thyroid. Years now.
Okay. How are your joints generally?
Joints are fine.
Let's get some numbers. Blood pressure first.
Righto, go for it.
134 over 82. Pulse 74. Temperature 36.7. Oxygen 98 percent. Breathing 14.
Is that all good, or is something off?
All unremarkable. Weight's 68 kilos, too. Now tip your head back for me, open wide.
Ahh.
The inside of your mouth is dry and sticky, and your tongue's quite smooth and red.
Now look up. Your eyes are a bit pink along the lids and there's very little moisture.
Yeah, that's what the mirror tells me.
So here's my thinking. This looks most likely like Sjogren's syndrome, an autoimmune condition that dries out the glands.
Autoimmune? That sounds serious.
It's common and very manageable, so try not to worry yet. I can't rule out your thyroid playing a part either, so we keep that in view.
Right.
Meantime, sip water through the day, and sugar-free lollies or gum help keep saliva flowing.
Easy enough. I've got a bottle on my desk anyway.
Take regular screen breaks at work too. Blinking more often helps the eyes.
I'll try that. Never thought about blinking.
Most people don't. I'd like to dig into this properly, so we'll sort the next steps at reception.
Sounds fine to me. Whatever you reckon.
Good on you. Thanks for coming in.
Cheers, doctor.
